idiom_name: class with a private std::mutex member; every operation starts with std::scoped_lock
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies both halves of the guardian: `std::mutex` is the lock and `std::scoped_lock` (C++17) or `std::lock_guard` is the RAII release that survives exceptions and early returns, so the pattern becomes a small class whose state is private and whose every operation begins by locking its own mutex member. What replaces the classic structure is the member discipline: the mutex must be a member of the guarded object (same lifetime, one lock per object, never a global), the guard must be a named local so it lives for the whole scope, and the class must never hand out references or iterators into its containers. `std::shared_mutex` (C++17) is the guardian's read-heavy form - that is the Read-Write Lock row - while `std::atomic` fields can replace the lock for a single scalar; both are choices hidden inside the class, which is the point.
pitfalls: Returning a reference, span or iterator into the guarded container hands callers the state; the guarded operation must copy out or run a callback under the lock.
`std::scoped_lock{mutex_};` as a temporary locks and immediately unlocks - the classic beginner error the standard documents; the guard needs a name.
Calling another guarded method from inside a critical section self-deadlocks with a plain std::mutex; std::recursive_mutex only hides the design problem.
